title: Move Sub-Tree of N-Ary Tree
statement:
You get `root`, the root of a tree in which a node may have any number of children, and two different nodes `p` and `q` of that tree. Every node has a unique integer `val` and an array `children` holding its child nodes from left to right. Move `p`, together with everything below it, so that it hangs from `q` as the **last** entry of `q.children`, and return the root of the tree afterwards. Three situations can occur:

- `p` is already one of `q`'s children: change nothing, wherever it sits in that list.
- `q` lies somewhere below `p`: moving `p` would cut the tree apart, so first unhook `q` (with its own subtree) from its parent, and put `q` in the exact slot that `p` occupied in `p`'s parent's `children`. If `p` was the root, `q` becomes the new root instead. Then append `p` to `q.children`.
- Otherwise (`p` lies below `q`, or neither lies below the other): take `p` out of its parent's `children` and append it to `q.children`.

Each case is written as `[root, p, q]`. `root` is the tree serialized breadth first: the root's value and a `null`, then, for every node in breadth-first order, its children's values followed by one `null` that closes the group (a leaf contributes only the `null`), with trailing `null`s left out. `p` and `q` are the values of the two nodes. Your function is called with the three node objects and returns the root node, which is shown in the same serialization. (The TypeScript starter types nodes as `_Node`, which does not list `children`; the objects still have it.)
constraints: The tree has between 2 and 1000 nodes
p and q are nodes of the tree
signature: Node moveSubTree(Node root, Node p, Node q)
notes:
## Intuition

Moving a subtree only changes a few child lists, so all the work is in learning two facts about the tree: the parent of every node, and whether `q` sits below `p`. One depth-first pass collects both. After that the three situations are a handful of list edits: unhooking a node from its parent's `children`, putting a node into a slot, and appending `p` to `q.children`.

## Approach

1. Run `dfs` from `root`, recording each child's parent in `parent` (the root's parent is `null`). The flag `insideP` is true for `p` and every node below it, so when the search reaches `q` it stores that flag in `qBelowP`.
2. If `parentOfP` is already `q`, return `root` untouched.
3. If `qBelowP`, remove `q` from `parentOfQ.children`, then put `q` where `p` was in `parentOfP.children`, or make `q` the new `root` when `p` had no parent.
4. Otherwise just remove `p` from `parentOfP.children`.
5. Append `p` to `q.children` and return `root`.

## Example 1, step by step

The tree is `1 → [2, 3]`, `2 → [4, 5]`, `3 → [6]`, `4 → [7, 8]`, with `p = 4` and `q = 1`. The search finds `parentOfP = 2`, and `q` (the root) is visited with `insideP = false`, so `qBelowP = false`. Node 2 is not `q`, so step 4 removes 4 from 2's children, leaving `2 → [5]`, and step 5 makes `1 → [2, 3, 4]`. Serialized: `[1,null,2,3,4,null,5,null,6,null,7,8]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one traversal, plus `indexOf` and `splice` on single child lists.
- Space: O(n) for the parent map and the recursion stack on a deep tree.

## Pitfalls

- When `p` is already a child of `q`, do nothing, even if it is not `q`'s last child.
- In the `q`-below-`p` case, detach `q` before appending `p`; otherwise `p` ends up inside its own subtree and the tree becomes a cycle.
- `q` takes `p`'s exact position among its siblings, not the end of the list, and becomes the root when `p` was the root.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `parent` | map from each node to its parent (`null` for the root) |
| `qBelowP` | whether `q` lies inside `p`'s subtree |
| `insideP` | whether the node being visited is `p` or below it |
| `parentOfP`, `parentOfQ` | the current parents of `p` and `q` |

narration.2: Map every node to its parent; the root has none.
narration.5: Visit node, knowing whether it is p or lies below p.
narration.6: Reaching q tells us which situation we are in.
narration.7: Remember whether q was found inside p's subtree.
narration.9: Look at each child in order.
narration.10: Record that this child hangs from node.
narration.11: Recurse; the flag turns on once we step onto p and stays on below it.
narration.15: Search the whole tree once, starting inside p only if the root is p.
narration.16: Look up p's current parent (null when p is the root).
narration.17: p is already q's child: the rules say leave the tree alone.
narration.20: q is below p, so moving p alone would detach the tree.
narration.22: Unhook q, with its subtree, from its old parent.
narration.26: Otherwise q takes over p's exact slot among its siblings.
narration.29: q is not below p: just unhook p from its parent.
narration.31: Hang p, with its whole subtree, as q's last child.
narration.32: Return the root, which only changes when p was the old root.
